decisions_log.detail: Executed and committed bf28aaf (CODEREF-CORE). Wave-1 scope = 3 files chosen on measured import fan-in from .coderef/graph.json. orchestrator.ts EXCLUDED despite ranking highest (fan-in 62) because its resource sheet grades WARN and a wave must start clean, or its first run reports a failure the wave did not cause. call-resolver.ts excluded for known api-complete drift. Checker moved not_applicable -> PASS 8 pass / 0 warn / 0 fail.

parseScopes() in the doc-code-tie checker keys LITERALLY on a level-2 heading spelled exactly 'Scopes'. The first draft of CORE's standard used 'Declared scope' and the ENTIRE kind silently reported not_applicable: standard present, scope table right there, nothing graded, exit 0. Nothing in that output distinguishes it from a project that declared no standard at all. A comment marking the heading load-bearing now sits in CORE's doc-code-tie.md. FOLLOW-UP CANDIDATE: the checker should WARN when it finds a doc-code-tie standard whose Scopes section it cannot locate, instead of silently grading nothing — a false not_applicable is indistinguishable from a true one, which is the same silent-failure class this kind exists to catch.

SELF-REPORTED DEFECT in this WO's own execution. The registry row was flipped to checkpoint_ready while communication.json still read plan_created and carried ZERO phase_transitions — for a WO whose work was fully committed and verified. The DB said ready-to-close, the disk said never executed, and neither was the truth. Repaired by writing the phase-1 transition (commit bf28aaf) and bringing the on-disk status UP to the truth rather than reverting the row down to a stale value. Cause: the registry write was done by hand at the end of execution instead of through the phase-transition writer, which updates both. The close-time scoped tracking-validator would likely have caught this, which is an argument for running it rather than trusting the executing agent to remember.
